description: Service-version ordering (mesh.md section 2.5). A pure-function fixture, not an envelope fixture: each case gives two declared service versions of ONE service and the exact outcome a conformant comparison MUST produce. Required only for ports that order service versions; a port implementing section 2.4 identity without section 2.5 ordering stays service-version conformant. The point of pinning this at all is that 'sortable' is not a specification and a comparator is — "10" and "9" order one way as integers and the opposite way as strings, so two ports that each infer a scheme will disagree about which release is newer inside a tool used to decide deployments. Hence: the scheme is declared and never inferred, there is no default, and the closed set is exactly integer/semver/lexicographic. `compare` cases assert the sign of comparing `left` against `right`: -1 (left is earlier), 0 (same position in the order), 1 (left is later), or the string "not-orderable" when the two carry different schemes. `parse` cases assert whether a value is valid under a declared scheme; an invalid one MUST be rejected where it is declared rather than carried and compared later. Ordering is defined only within one service, and order is not lineage — a later version is not thereby a superset, a successor, or safe to substitute.

compare.name: integer-orders-by-value-not-by-string
compare.comment: The case the whole fixture exists for. Lexicographically "10" < "9"; numerically 10 > 9. A port that infers the scheme from the value gets this backwards and reports a rollback as an upgrade.

compare.name: integer-same-build-is-same-position
compare.comment: Same position in the order. NOT an assertion that the two are the same version — section 2.4 is explicit that identity is extrinsic and that two releases may declare byte-identical contracts.

compare.name: integer-ignores-leading-zeros
compare.comment: A zero-padded build number from a pipeline that formats its counter. Numerically equal, so equal in the order.

compare.name: integer-is-arbitrary-precision
compare.comment: Build counters outrun 64-bit signed integers in no real pipeline, but a comparator that silently overflows is worse than one that refuses, so the required behaviour is stated rather than left to the port's integer width.

compare.name: semver-prerelease-is-earlier-than-its-release
compare.comment: SemVer 2.0.0 section 11: a pre-release version has lower precedence than the normal version it precedes.

compare.name: semver-prerelease-numeric-identifiers-compare-numerically
compare.comment: rc.10 is later than rc.9 — the same digits-versus-string trap as the integer scheme, one level down.

compare.name: semver-build-metadata-is-ignored-in-precedence
compare.comment: SemVer 2.0.0 section 10: build metadata is ignored when determining precedence. Two builds differing only in metadata occupy the same position in the order — which is exactly why order is not identity.

compare.name: lexicographic-does-not-rescue-numbers
compare.comment: Under `lexicographic` the string answer IS the right answer, because that is what the operator declared. The scheme is a promise about how the values were minted, not a hint to be second-guessed.

compare.name: mixed-schemes-are-not-orderable
compare.comment: A service that switched from build numbers to SemVer has a real discontinuity in its history. Ordering across it would be a claim no data supports, so the outcome is reported rather than guessed. A normal outcome, not an error.

compare.name: mixed-schemes-are-not-orderable-even-when-both-values-parse-as-integers
compare.comment: Both values would parse under either scheme. It is still not orderable: the schemes disagree, and agreeing by accident on one pair of values is not an order.

compare.name: an-undeclared-scheme-is-not-orderable
compare.comment: mesh.md section 2.5: there is no default scheme. A serviceVersion declared without one is an identity, not a position in an order, and a port MUST NOT invent a comparison for it.

parse.name: integer-rejects-a-semver-value
parse.comment: The build that declared this is the cheapest place in the system to catch it. Carrying it and discovering the mismatch at comparison time means the wrong answer reaches a reader.

parse.name: lexicographic-rejects-empty
parse.comment: An empty serviceVersion is section 2.4 case 3 — no declared version at all — not a version that happens to be blank.

parse.name: an-unknown-scheme-is-rejected
parse.comment: The set is closed. A port meeting a scheme it does not know MUST reject it rather than fall back to string comparison, because a silent fallback is indistinguishable from a correct answer.
